title: Protein powder from freeze-dried food: what's documented.
description: Two manufacturer posts describe blending a shake and drying it. No extension source addresses protein powder at all. What that leaves documented.

faq.question: Does freeze-drying concentrate the protein in food?
faq.answer: No source documents a concentration effect. Sublimation removes water, so the dried result is more protein by weight than the liquid it came from, but the measured protein-percent-by-weight change through a home cycle is unpublished. Both Harvest Right protein pages describe blending a shake and drying it, not concentrating anything [1][2].

faq.question: Can you freeze-dry store-bought protein powder on its own?
faq.answer: No manufacturer or extension source addresses drying a commercial powder. The published route runs the other way: make a liquid shake from the powder, dry the shake, then grind it [1]. Protein powder also has no entry on Harvest Right's time chart [3].

faq.question: How long does a home-made shake powder keep?
faq.answer: No protein-powder-specific figure exists. Harvest Right's 25-year claim attaches to mylar with an oxygen absorber, kept cool, dark and below 85°F, and is conditioned on fat content [14]; Utah State University Extension says no real data exists on home freeze-dried shelf life [15], and UC ANR does not recommend consuming home freeze-dried products beyond 5 to 10 years [16].

faq.question: Is a dried shake safe if the milk was raw?
faq.answer: Utah State University Extension classifies raw milk and raw dairy as high-risk and answers no without pasteurization, because unpasteurized dairy can harbor Listeria, Salmonella or E. coli and the process does not pasteurize [10]. Freeze-drying is a preservation process, not a kill step.

howTo.name: Blend the shake first
howTo.text: Harvest Right's published method starts with a made shake — milk plus protein powder plus whatever else the recipe calls for — not with dry ingredients [1].

howTo.name: Pour onto the tray
howTo.text: The blended liquid goes onto the tray. Liquids are among the loads manufacturers pair with liners and with pre-freezing, though no protein-specific tray depth or pre-freeze time is published [1].

howTo.name: Run the cycle
howTo.text: No cycle time is published for a protein shake by any source, and protein powder has no entry on the manufacturer time chart [3]. Confirm dryness by the break test or by weighing the tray until the weight stops changing [12][13].

howTo.name: Grind and package
howTo.text: Grind the dried sheet back into a powder [1], then package into mylar with an oxygen absorber, which is the condition the long storage claims are attached to [14].

bodyHtml:
The short version: Freeze-drying does not concentrate protein — it removes water, and the protein that is left is the protein that went in. The only published home method is a manufacturer's do-it-yourself route: blend a protein shake, dry it, grind it back to a powder [1][2]. No extension service addresses protein powder at all, and no source publishes a cycle time, a yield, or a storage life for it.

What is actually published

Two Harvest Right blog posts are the entire first-party record: a current page on freeze-drying protein shakes [1] and a 2015 post on freeze-drying protein [2]. Neither describes a concentration effect. Both describe recombination — you make the shake first, then dry what you made.

Everything else is an absence, and the absences are the substance of this page.

QuestionWhat is publishedSource
Is there a method?Yes, as a make-your-own process: blend a shake, pour it on the tray, dry, grind the resultHarvest Right [1]
Does it concentrate protein?No manufacturer claims this. Both protein pages describe shake recombination, not concentration[1][2]
Cycle timeNot published. Protein powder has no entry on Harvest Right's freeze-drying time chart[3]
Fresh-to-dried yieldNot published for protein powder in any form—
Rehydration ratio"Add water" to the finished shake powder. No measured ratio[1]
Storage lifeNo protein-powder-specific figure from any source—
Extension guidanceNone. No extension service addresses protein powder as a subject—
Top-tier home-preservation guidanceThe National Center for Home Food Preservation publishes no freeze-drying guidance at all; its freezing and drying pages cover conventional freezing and dehydrators[4][5]

Why "concentration" is the wrong word

Raw foods run 80 to 95 percent water, and sublimation is what a freeze dryer removes — around 90 percent of the moisture in the primary phase plus another 1 to 2 percent in desorption, by the University of Minnesota Extension's account [7]. What sublimation does not touch is fat: "Freeze drying removes water, but oil remains," in Harvest Right's own words [6].

So the powder that comes off the tray is more protein by weight than the liquid that went on, in the same way that any dried food is more of everything by weight. The protein-percent-by-weight change through a home cycle has not been measured or published by anyone. Treating a dried shake as a concentrate is an inference, not a documented result.

The nearest published yield figure in the whole dairy category is for milk, and it comes from a secondary source rather than a manufacturer or an extension service: about 20 percent for whole milk (a gallon yielding roughly five cups of powder) and about 16 percent for skim, with a gallon taking roughly 30 hours on a large unit [8]. That is a milk figure. It is not a protein-shake figure, and nobody publishes one.

The base ingredients carry the documented risks

A protein shake is mostly a dairy or dairy-substitute liquid, so the dairy record applies to it.

  • Freeze-drying is not a kill step. Utah State University Extension classifies raw milk, raw cheese and raw dairy as high-risk and answers "No" without pasteurization, because unpasteurized dairy can harbor Listeria, Salmonella or E. coli and the process does not pasteurize anything [10].
  • Fat rides along. The University of Minnesota Extension puts it plainly: home freeze-drying "works well for…proteins, but not for foods that are high in fat" [7]. Harvest Right agrees on the storage consequence: "Foods that contain higher amounts of fat generally have shorter storage lives" [14]. A shake built on whole milk, nut butter or added oils sits on the wrong side of that line; no source publishes a numeric fat ceiling for any food.
  • Dried dairy is not inert. The 1952 Journal of Dairy Science work on freeze-dried milk found that "the fat emulsion of freeze-dried powder is partially destabilized," and that the powder "frequently acquires a fruity flavor" [11]. That is research-scale equipment from a 1952 process, not a consumer unit — but it is the only peer-reviewed description of the product in this family.

Calling it dry, and calling it stored

The dryness endpoint for a powder is the same one published for everything else, and it is worth quoting because a poured liquid dries from the surface inward. Harvest Right: "The outside of a piece of food can feel completely dry even when moisture remains in the center" [12]. The published check is to break pieces open, inspect the center for moisture, cold spots, softness or a darker color, and test the thickest pieces from several trays [12]. Stay Fresh publishes the alternative that suits a tray of liquid better: weigh the tray at cycle end and again after extended drying, and "if the weight remains consistent, this indicates that the food is adequately dry" [13].

On storage life, the manufacturer and extension records disagree, and neither is about protein powder specifically. Harvest Right attaches its 25-year figure to mylar with an oxygen absorber, kept cool, dark, dry and below 85°F, and conditions it explicitly on fat content [14]. Utah State University Extension's position is that "no real data exists on the shelf-life of home freeze-dried products" [15], and UC ANR states the 25-year claim "has not been corroborated by university studies for home freeze dryers" and that consuming home freeze-dried products "is not recommended beyond 5–10 years after processing" [16]. USU's own food-by-food guide lands in the same 5-to-10-year place for home product [10]. No figure here is a shelf-life promise, and none of them were written about a dried shake.

Packaging is where the fat caution and the storage guidance meet: mylar plus an oxygen absorber is the condition attached to the long claims [14]. Our Freeze-Drying Packaging Starter Kit (100 mylar bags in three sizes, 100 absorbers, labels) covers that step. Sold by Sublime Pantry.

Reconstituting it

Harvest Right's instruction for the finished shake powder is to add water [1]. For dried dairy generally the same publisher says to "add water gradually and stir until it returns to its original state" [9]. No measured powder-to-water ratio is published for a protein shake by any source, which means the ratio you settle on is your own, arrived at by adjustment rather than by a documented figure.

What we could not source

  • Any manufacturer claim of protein concentration. Searched both Harvest Right protein pages [1][2] directly; both describe do-it-yourself shake recombination, and neither claims concentration.
  • The measured protein-percent-by-weight change through a home cycle. Unpublished by anyone, at any tier.
  • A cycle time for protein powder. Harvest Right's time chart carries no entry for it, alongside no entry for eggs or ice cream [3].
  • Fresh-to-dried yield. No extension service publishes a yield percentage for any food. Across the whole dairy strand exactly one figure exists, for milk, from a secondary source [8].
  • Any extension guidance on protein powder. None found at any extension service.
  • The National Center for Home Food Preservation's position. It has no freeze-drying publication; the freezing and drying pages cover conventional freezing and dehydrators only [4][5], and its freeze-drying educator page is subscriber-gated.
  • A numeric fat threshold. No source at any tier gives a fat ceiling for any food. The preference for lean is qualitative everywhere it appears.
  • A residual-moisture target. Every published moisture figure is framed as percent removed, never percent remaining.
